source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Active inference treats reward as just another observation with a prior preference. Policies are scored by expected free energy, which mixes extrinsic value (preferred outcomes) and epistemic value (expected information gain). With flat preferences the agent still explores out of curiosity.
numbers: No fixed N. Illustrated on a modified FrozenLake grid world; simulations show behaviour with the reward removed.
limits: Illustration, not a benchmark. Compares with RL conceptually. The reward-free result depends on the agent having an explicit generative model.
agent_relevance: S7 can be written as one score: value of a test = how much it is expected to cut uncertainty about hypotheses, plus how much it helps the goal. With no goal signal, the epistemic term alone still ranks tests.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2020) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: In the FrozenLake demo with the reward signal removed, an RL agent has a flat value function and no reason to act, while the active inference agent keeps exploring to resolve uncertainty about hidden states.
numbers: Qualitative simulation; no effect sizes in the text read.
limits: Toy environment. Does not show active inference beats RL when reward is present.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that scores tests by information gain still works when there is no external pass/fail signal.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2020) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: The expected free energy is not simply the variational free energy evaluated in the future. A functional that is the natural extension of free energy actively discourages exploration. So exploration does not follow from free energy minimisation alone; it comes from the epistemic term built into EFE.
numbers: Theory plus small simulations. Proposes a new objective, the Free-Energy of the Expected Future (FEEF), which keeps the epistemic term and is a divergence between predicted and desired futures.
quote: it is not simply "the free energy in the future"
limits: Critique by authors inside the field. FEEF is not widely adopted.
agent_relevance: Minimising surprise alone would make an agent avoid informative tests. The information-gain term must be explicit in the S7 rule.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2020) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: EFE splits into an extrinsic term (goal-directed, from preferences) and the expected information gain (epistemic value). The same quantity also splits as risk plus ambiguity; the two forms are mathematically equivalent.
numbers: Appendix lists many equivalent decompositions.
limits: Equivalence holds under the discrete POMDP generative model assumed.
agent_relevance: Pick the decomposition that is cheap to compute. For hypothesis testing, expected information gain is an entropy difference that code can count.

source: Markovic, Stojic, Schwobel, Kiebel (2021) An empirical evaluation of active inference in multi-armed bandits
finding: Approximate active inference was compared with Bayesian UCB and optimistic Thompson sampling. In stationary bandits it did not give efficient long-term behaviour. In switching (non-stationary) bandits it did substantially better than both.
numbers: Stationary case, K=10 arms, ensemble of N=1000 agents: active inference beat the bandit algorithms only up to about T=10^4 trials (text reads 'T = 104'), then cumulative regret grew faster than logarithmic. Switching bandit compared on regret rate.
limits: Performance depends on preference precision lambda; lambda fixed at 0.25 by visual inspection in one comparison. Simulation only, no humans.
agent_relevance: Information-driven choice pays off when the world changes. On a fixed puzzle with stable hypotheses, simpler rules can match it. Do not claim a universal win.

source: Markovic, Stojic, Schwobel, Kiebel (2021) An empirical evaluation of active inference in multi-armed bandits
finding: Exact active inference (full planning) and the approximate version were compared. Both are sensitive to the preference-precision parameter; in switching bandits the regret-rate minimum is stable over a range of lambda.
numbers: Figures and ensemble statistics only.
limits: The exact version is too costly beyond small problems, so most tests used the approximation.
agent_relevance: The weight between pragmatic and epistemic terms is a tuned knob. If our agent weights them, the weight needs a test, not a guess ([D] status).

source: de Vries et al. (2025) Expected Free Energy-based Planning as Variational Inference
finding: EFE planning can be recast as minimising a single variational free energy on a generative model with preference and epistemic priors, solved by message passing. The abstract says the computational burden of EFE minimisation had been a major obstacle to scalability.
numbers: Theory and demonstration; no benchmark numbers read.
limits: No LLM test. Epistemic priors must be added to the model by hand.
agent_relevance: Confirms the cost objection. Scoring every candidate test by full EFE is expensive, so S7 should score a short list of tests, not all.

source: Prakki (2024) Active Inference for Self-Organizing Multi-LLM Systems
finding: An active inference layer chooses prompts and search strategies for an LLM research agent. It picks among 33 prompt combinations and 11 search strategies by expected free energy, with state and parameter information gain switched on.
numbers: Observation model: 7 modalities, quality scored 0-10 by GPT-4o-mini through JSON. Policy horizon 2, inference horizon 1, learning rate 50, policy precision 8, action precision 16, deterministic selection.
limits: Simulated environment. The LLM supplies the scores the agent treats as observations, so the judge is the same family as the worker.
agent_relevance: The only case found of EFE selecting actions inside an LLM loop. It selects prompts, not hypothesis tests. Judged scores as observations conflict with G2 (revise only from real output).

source: Prakki (2024) Active Inference for Self-Organizing Multi-LLM Systems
finding: Reported results are qualitative: learned observation matrices move from uniform to structured, and EFE shifts from early information gathering to targeted prompt testing.
numbers: No accuracy, win rate or baseline comparison in the text read; results are shown in figures.
limits: No control arm (fixed or random prompts) found, so the claim of effectiveness is unproven.
agent_relevance: Treat as a design sketch, not evidence that EFE selection helps an LLM agent.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Enhancing LLMs with Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: Open LLMs ask low-information questions in 20 Questions. Preference optimisation (DPO) on pairs of high-EIG vs low-EIG questions raised success and cut questions. Plain fine-tuning on high-EIG dialogues did not help success.
numbers: LLaMA-2-Chat 7B, INLG set: zero-shot S@1 56.7%, 7.1 questions, EIG 0.34; fine-tune 46.6%, 4.6, 0.41; DPO 68.9%, 5.2, 0.45.
limits: One 7B model. Training data self-annotated by the same model. Candidate set must be closed so EIG can be computed.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that raising question EIG raises success, even for a weak model. Supports S7 pick-by-EIG, though here it is done by training, not by scaffold.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Enhancing LLMs with Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: DPO gains carried to other domains. Things set: zero-shot 51.1% S@1, 7.5 questions, EIG 0.29; DPO 61.1%, 5.2, 0.40. Celebrities: zero-shot 71.1%, 7.6, 0.35; DPO 72.2%, 5.1, 0.47.
numbers: Gains: INLG +12.2 points, Things +10 points, Celebrities only +1.1 points (but about 2.5 fewer questions).
limits: Celebrities success barely moved, so benefit depends on the domain.
agent_relevance: Expect a smaller gain where the model already knows the domain well.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Enhancing LLMs with Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: Boundary conditions: with larger or open candidate sets the gain shrinks and EIG can fall. INLG16: S@1 44.4 to 51.1%. BigBench: 17.2 to 31.0% but EIG 0.31 to 0.28. Concrete targets 25.0 to 37.5%; abstract targets 7.7 to 23.1% with EIG 0.29 to 0.24 and more questions (9.3 to 10.3).
numbers: BigBench concrete and abstract subsets are small test sets.
limits: EIG falling while success rises shows EIG is a proxy; part of the success came from better guesses.
agent_relevance: Open hypothesis spaces break exact EIG. The agent must first list hypotheses (a state) before S7 can count.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: BED-LLM picks the next question by estimated expected information gain from the LLM's own predictive distributions. On 20 Questions across several LLMs it raised success by 37.4 percentage points on average over direct prompting, more than doubled it in over half the setups, and never decreased it.
numbers: Animals, Celebrities, Things, 100 targets each; GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Large, Qwen2.5-72B. Open target space (no list given to the model).
quote: BED-LLM's final success rate is typically more than double that of Prompt-Only
limits: Needs many LLM calls per turn: Qwen2.5-72B on the Animals set took about 2.5 hours for BED-LLM against under 1 hour for prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for S7 as expected information gain inside an inference-only loop. The gain is large for weak and strong models.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Raw in-context belief updating fails: even GPT-4o samples hypotheses that conflict with past answers and becomes overconfident as history grows. BED-LLM filters hypotheses for compatibility with history and keeps them diverse.
numbers: Described in the method section; no single headline number for this failure.
limits: The compatibility check is itself done by the LLM.
agent_relevance: Matches G2/G3: keep the hypothesis list under code control and check each hypothesis against recorded answers.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Ablations: predictive entropy instead of true EIG is the strongest alternative. Letting the LLM judge the best question from the same candidates (Implicit Maximization) still beats prompt-only and is cheap. Unfiltered beliefs do worse than entropy.
numbers: Ranking read from prose; Table 1 values were not captured. Entropy performs close to the Split baseline, so the gain comes from proper EIG with a non-deterministic likelihood.
limits: Ranking only, no numbers.
agent_relevance: A cheap S7 (model asked to pick the most separating test) already helps. A counted EIG adds more.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Updating the likelihood with the full history made results worse than a static likelihood in most cells. Static vs updating, success %: Animals Qwen 95 vs 89, GPT-4o 93 vs 86, GPT-4o-mini 88 vs 85; Celebrities Qwen 84 vs 70, Llama-3.3-70B 55 vs 44; Things GPT-4o 64 vs 57.
numbers: Standard errors about 2-5 points. Two cells reversed: Llama-3.1-8B Animals 63 vs 67, Llama-3.3-70B Animals 79 vs 80.
limits: Reason given by the authors: context-induced calibration shift.
agent_relevance: Score each test on a fresh, history-free prompt. Do not let the long thread colour the probability that a test splits the hypotheses.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Preference elicitation (movies): 200 user profiles, 5 turns, 10 recommendations rated 1-5 by an LLM judge. BED-LLM beat Prompt-Only and Entropy, but prompt-only was a stronger baseline here than in 20 Questions.
numbers: N=200 profiles; gains clearest when the questioner and answerer are different model families.
limits: Judge is an LLM; targets are abstract, so the benefit is smaller than in 20 Questions.
agent_relevance: Information gain helps less when hypotheses are fuzzy and cannot be listed.

source: Handa et al. (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN uses Bayesian optimal experimental design to pick which feature question to ask and an LLM to turn it into natural language. In a human study on content recommendation it beat LM-only open-ended and pairwise questioning and earlier BOED methods.
numbers: Human user study; 15 pairwise comparisons per participant; metric is time-integrated delta accuracy (TIDA). Exact figures not captured in the text read.
limits: LM open-ended questions beat LM pairwise questions, but OPEN's prediction step was the larger benefit. One domain.
agent_relevance: Same split of labour as our design: code scores the question, the model only phrases it.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT has the LLM simulate future answer branches, scores each question by information gain, and propagates rewards to pick the best question. It raised task success by 38.1% on average over direct prompting across LLMs on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Five datasets. Llama3-70B gain 46.6%. Beats CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, original ToT by 28.3%, adapted ToT by 12.4%.
limits: Relative percentages as reported; base success rates differ by dataset.
agent_relevance: A tree-search form of S7 works in LLM agents and beats self-consistency and reflection on these tasks.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Specific results: GPT-4 diagnosis (DX) 97.0% success; MedDG 81.4% (Gemini-1.5-Pro) and 88.0% (GPT-4); troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3% with 7.8 questions. In 20 Questions, CoT and PP prompting did worse than GPT-4 alone.
numbers: Simplified medical tasks; closed question sets (CS) give the headline scores; open-set (OS) scores are lower.
limits: Simplified diagnosis, answerer is an LLM, not real patients.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought alone can hurt question choice, fitting G1 and our word-puzzle finding that forced reasoning adds noise.

source: Grand, Pepe, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People
finding: Collaborative Battleship with N=42 human players versus LM agents. Asking questions correlates with human performance (rho=0.684). Many LMs ask redundant or uninformative questions and answer inaccurately.
numbers: Human answer accuracy 92.5%. LM answer accuracy from 52.5% (GPT-4o-mini) to 92.8%; o3, o4-mini and GPT-5 meet or exceed mean human accuracy.
limits: Grid game with a clear hypothesis space.
agent_relevance: A human reference for good information seeking, on a task where LM weakness is in questions, not in reasoning.

source: Grand, Pepe, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People
finding: Adding Bayesian strategies for questions, moves and decisions lifts weak models to above human level. Targeting F1: Llama-4-Scout 0.367 to 0.764, GPT-4o 0.450 to 0.782, GPT-5 0.716 baseline. Win rate 0.82-0.83 vs humans and 0.67 vs GPT-5, at about 1% of GPT-5's cost.
numbers: Captain agents, max 15 questions and 40 moves; replicated on Guess Who.
limits: Needs an explicit board model for Monte Carlo sampling of hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Counting information gain let a cheap model beat a frontier model. Scaffold beat scale on this task.

source: Grand, Pepe, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People
finding: Question quality in bits: Bayesian question selection raised EIG by up to 0.227 bits per question (94.2% of the ceiling of 0.531 bits). Redundant (EIG=0) questions fell from 18.5% to 0.2% (Llama-4-Scout) and 14.6% to 1.2% (GPT-4o). Human mean EIG 0.351, median 0.411.
numbers: Per-question EIG; ceiling set by the noise setting in the game.
limits: Humans are themselves below the ceiling.
agent_relevance: Redundant tests are the main waste. A cheap check that a test splits the hypotheses (EIG above 0) removes most of it.

source: Grand, Pepe, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People
finding: LMs degrade on context-dependent questions where humans do not. Humans: 92.8% simple, 91.9% complex. Code generation (answering by program) gave +14.7 points over base; best model o3 still 87.4% on complex questions.
numbers: Spotter accuracy; Llama-4-Scout drops from 68.0% on simple questions.
limits: Task specific.
agent_relevance: Have code, not the model, work out how a test splits the hypotheses.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2024) Active Preference Inference using Language Models and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Out-of-the-box instruction-tuned LLMs ask uninformative preference questions. An inference-time algorithm that samples 8 candidate questions and picks by expected entropy reduction and expected model change does better with fewer user turns in a web-shopping task.
numbers: Binary reward: entropy-reduction LLM clearly beats baselines after more than one question; its three-question score exceeds the baselines' four-question score. Confidence intervals over 150 samples.
limits: Simplified shopping setting, simulated user; exact accuracy not captured.
agent_relevance: Early example of the sample-then-rank-by-information pattern for S7, with a small budget.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-Frugal Cognition as Active Inference Under Uncertain Precision
finding: Theory: EFE minimisation under uncertain precision stops after k high-validity cues and equals take-the-best. Prediction: more chain-of-thought hurts on items with high meta-uncertainty. A pre-registered test found the effect.
numbers: 7,875 responses; benchmark FEH-79; high-regime accuracy drop 17.3 points (95% credible interval 7.7 to 25.5); matched control items with definite answers show no cost.
limits: Not universal: decisive in mid-to-large models, directional in the two frontier models, absent or reversed in the two weakest. Single author, preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Supports a stop rule: when the reliability of evidence is unknown, stop adding reasoning and decide (G1, no forced reasoning on a schedule).

source: Wen (2025) A Framework for Inherently Safer AGI through Language-Mediated Active Inference
finding: A proposal combining active inference with LLMs; exploration is driven by expected information gain of actions. Seen only through a search summary; full text not read.
numbers: No experiments seen.
limits: Not opened; unverified detail.
agent_relevance: Conceptual only; no measured result to use.
